t: #3388 Count Beautiful Splits in an Array
o: Count cuts i < j (nums1 = nums[0:i], nums2 = nums[i:j], nums3 = nums[j:n], all non-empty) such that nums1 is a prefix of nums2, or nums2 is a prefix of nums3. In Example 1 ([1,1,2,1]): cut (1,2) makes nums1=[1] a prefix of nums2=[1,2]; cut (1,3) makes nums1=[1] a prefix of nums2=[1]; both beautiful → 2. With n up to 5000 there are ~12.5M (i,j) pairs, so an O(n²) algorithm with O(1) prefix checks is required — naive prefix comparison per pair would be O(n³).
k: Precompute lcp[i][j] = length of the longest common prefix of suffixes starting at i and j via reverse DP: lcp[i][j] = (nums[i]==nums[j]) ? lcp[i+1][j+1]+1 : 0.
Condition 1 (nums1 prefix of nums2) is lcp[0][i] ≥ i; condition 2 (nums2 prefix of nums3) is lcp[i][j] ≥ j − i.
With the LCP table, each (i, j) pair is judged in O(1), giving O(n²) total.

a.n: Approach 1: LCP Table DP + Pair Counting
a.i: The classic suffix-comparison table lets us test 'is A a prefix of B' instantly. Build lcp bottom-right to top-left, then double-loop over all valid split points adding 1 whenever either prefix condition holds.
s: Allocate lcp of size (n+1)×(n+1), initialized to 0.
Fill lcp[i][j] = lcp[i+1][j+1] + 1 if nums[i] == nums[j], else 0, iterating i and j downward.
For each i in [1, n−2] and j in [i+1, n−1]: if lcp[0][i] ≥ i or lcp[i][j] ≥ j − i, increment the count.
a.t: O(n²) — building the LCP table and scanning all (i, j) pairs are each quadratic.
a.sp: O(n²) for the LCP table (~25M entries at n = 5000; use short/int32 to stay within limits).

a.n: Approach 2: Rolling Hash + Binary Search LCP
a.i: Replace the big table with polynomial hashing: the LCP of two suffixes is found by binary searching the largest k with equal hashes of prefixes of length k. This uses O(n) memory at the cost of an extra log factor.
s: Precompute prefix hashes and powers of a base modulo a large prime.
getHash(l, k) returns the hash of nums[l..l+k-1] in O(1).
lcpQuery(a, b) binary searches the largest k ≤ min(n−a, n−b) with matching hashes.
Run the same double loop over (i, j), calling lcpQuery for the needed comparisons.
a.t: O(n² log n) — the pair loop performs O(1)–O(log n) hash comparisons per pair.
a.sp: O(n) for hash and power arrays.

w: Lead with the LCP-table approach — it's the intended O(n²) solution and easiest to explain. Pitfalls: off-by-one on split boundaries (all three parts non-empty means 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n−1), confusing 'prefix of' direction (condition 1 compares suffix 0 with suffix i, condition 2 compares suffix i with suffix j), and memory blowup of the table in Java (use short or byte-packed arrays). Follow-ups: count splits under both conditions simultaneously, or handle streaming input where the LCP table doesn't fit.
